items.q: Which is NOT one of the four informal measures of a good relation schema?
options: Maximizing the number of NULL values
items.explain: The four measures are: clear semantics, reduce redundancy/anomalies, REDUCE (not maximize) NULLs, and avoid spurious tuples.

items.q: Being unable to add a project until an employee is assigned to it (because the PK can't be NULL) is which anomaly?
items.explain: Insertion anomaly: you can't insert valid data because unrelated required (key) data is missing. Deletion loses data; modification requires many redundant updates.

items.q: If only 15% of employees have an office, the best design per Guideline 3 is to:
options: Put Office_number in a separate relation EMP_OFFICES(Essn, Office_number) for only those who have one
Store offices as a multivalued attribute
items.explain: Guideline 3: minimize NULLs. An attribute NULL for most rows belongs in a separate relation keyed by the PK, holding only the applicable tuples.

items.q: Spurious tuples on a join are avoided by Guideline 4 by:
options: Joining only on (primary key, foreign key) pairs
items.explain: Joining on non-key matching attributes produces spurious tuples. Designing so joins occur on PK-FK pairs guarantees the lossless (non-additive) join property.

items.q: The functional dependency X → Y means:
options: For any two tuples, if they agree on X they must agree on Y
X and Y have the same values
items.explain: X → Y: whenever t1[X] = t2[X], then t1[Y] = t2[Y]. X functionally determines Y; the X-value pins down the Y-value.

items.q: Can a functional dependency be proven to hold by examining one relation state?
options: Yes, if it holds in that state it always holds
No — a state can only DISPROVE (rule out) an FD, never prove one
Only for relations with no NULLs
items.explain: An FD is a semantic constraint on ALL legal states. One state satisfying it doesn't guarantee it always will; but a counterexample (same X, different Y) rules it out.

items.q: A candidate key differs from a superkey in that a candidate key is:
items.explain: A superkey uniquely identifies rows but may carry extra attributes; a candidate key is a minimal superkey — removing any attribute breaks uniqueness.

items.q: A prime attribute is one that:
options: Is a member of some candidate key
Appears on the RHS of an FD
items.explain: A prime attribute belongs to at least one candidate key. A non-prime attribute is in no candidate key. (Distinct from being THE primary key.)

items.q: `{Ssn, Pnumber} → Hours` where neither Ssn nor Pnumber alone determines Hours is a:
items.explain: Full FD: removing any attribute from the LHS breaks it. Since neither part alone determines Hours, the whole key is required — a full dependency.

items.q: A partial dependency (the 2NF killer) can only occur when:
options: The primary/candidate key is composite (multiple attributes)
items.explain: A partial dependency is a non-prime attribute depending on PART of a key — only possible if the key has multiple attributes. Single-attribute keys can't have partial dependencies.

items.q: The dependency pattern that violates 3NF (transitive dependency) is:
items.explain: A transitive dependency is key → (non-prime) → (non-prime). If the middle attribute is a candidate key, it's allowed; the forbidden case is a non-prime determining a non-prime.

items.q: `ABC → BC` is an example of a:
items.explain: A trivial FD has Y ⊆ X. Here BC ⊆ ABC, so ABC → BC holds automatically (reflexive rule) and conveys no real constraint.

items.q: Which are Armstrong's three axioms?
items.explain: Armstrong's axioms: IR1 Reflexive (Y⊆X ⟹ X→Y), IR2 Augmentation (X→Y ⟹ XZ→YZ), IR3 Transitive (X→Y, Y→Z ⟹ X→Z). The others are derived.

items.q: Armstrong's axioms being 'sound and complete' means they:
options: Generate only valid FDs (sound) AND all valid FDs (complete)
items.explain: Sound = every inferred FD actually holds; complete = every FD that holds can be inferred. Hence repeatedly applying them yields the full closure F+.

items.q: Which is a VALID inference?
options: X → A and Y → B implies XY → AB
X → A and X → B implies X → AB (union)
X → AB implies XA → B only
items.explain: Union (same LHS): X→A and X→B give X→AB. You may split/combine the RHS, but you cannot split the LHS, and you cannot union FDs with different LHSs.

items.q: The proposed rule 'if α→β and γ→β then α→γ' is:
options: NOT sound — two determinants of β need not determine each other
items.explain: This rule is unsound (Silberschatz 7.26): two different attribute sets can both determine β without determining each other. A counterexample relation disproves it.

items.q: If the closure X⁺ equals all attributes of R, then X is:
items.explain: X⁺ = R means X determines every attribute, so X is a superkey. This is the standard test for keys.

items.q: For R(A,B,C,D,E,F,G) with F = {A→BC, BC→DE, D→F, CF→G}, what is {B,C}⁺?
items.explain: BC → DE adds D,E; D→F adds F; CF→G adds G. BC⁺ = {B,C,D,E,F,G}. A is not added (nothing determines A).

items.q: To check whether an FD X → Y holds under F, you:
options: Compute X⁺ and check if Y ⊆ X⁺
Check if X is a key
items.explain: X → Y holds iff Y is a subset of X⁺. Computing the attribute closure is far cheaper than enumerating F⁺.

items.q: Why do we use attribute closures and minimal covers instead of listing F⁺ directly?
options: F⁺ can be enormous — up to 2^(2^n) FDs for n attributes
items.explain: For n attributes there are up to 2^n · 2^n = 2^(2^n) possible FDs, so F⁺ is impractical to list. Closures and covers capture the same information compactly.

items.q: F covers E means:
options: Every FD in E can be inferred from F (E ⊆ F⁺)
F has more FDs than E
items.explain: F covers E if every dependency in E is in F⁺ — F can reproduce all of E's constraints.

items.q: Two FD sets E and F are equivalent when:
options: They have the same number of FDs
F covers E AND E covers F (E⁺ = F⁺)
items.explain: Equivalence requires mutual cover: every FD of E inferable from F and vice versa, so E⁺ = F⁺. Checking only one direction is a common error.

items.q: To test whether F covers G, for each FD X→Y in G you:
options: Compute X⁺ using F and check Y ⊆ X⁺
items.explain: Take each FD of G, compute the closure of its LHS using F, and verify the RHS is contained. If all pass, F covers G.

items.q: Which is NOT a condition of a minimal cover?
options: Every FD has a single attribute on the RHS
No FD has an extraneous LHS attribute
Every FD has two attributes on the LHS
items.explain: The three conditions are: single-attribute RHS, no extraneous LHS attribute, no redundant FD. There is no requirement about LHS size.

items.q: An attribute is extraneous in an FD if:
options: Removing it doesn't change the closure of the FD set
items.explain: An extraneous attribute can be removed without changing F⁺ (the set's meaning). Removing extraneous LHS attributes is step 2 of the minimal-cover algorithm.

items.q: The correct order of the minimal-cover algorithm is:
options: Remove redundant → split RHS → reduce LHS
Split RHS (canonical) → reduce LHS extraneous → remove redundant FDs
Reduce LHS → remove redundant → split RHS
items.explain: First put FDs in canonical form (single RHS), then remove extraneous LHS attributes, then remove redundant FDs — using the current reduced set at each closure check.

items.q: Is the minimal cover of a set of FDs unique?
options: No — a set can have several minimal covers depending on reduction order
Only if there are no transitive FDs
items.explain: Different reduction orders can yield different (but equivalent) minimal covers. Hence we say 'a' minimal cover, not 'the'.

items.q: An 'essential' attribute when finding candidate keys is one that:
options: Appears on the RHS of every FD
Appears on the RHS of NO FD (so must be in every candidate key)
items.explain: An attribute on no RHS cannot be determined by anything else, so it must belong to every candidate key. Start key-finding from the essential attributes.

items.q: R(A,B,C,D,E,F), F = {C→F, E→A, EC→D, A→B}. The candidate key is:
items.explain: Essential attributes (on no RHS) are C and E. CE⁺ = {C,E,F,A,D,B} = R, so CE is the (only) candidate key.

items.q: If R has n attributes and a single candidate key of size x, the number of superkeys is:
items.explain: The key must be in every superkey; the remaining n−x attributes are each independently in or out, giving 2^(n−x) superkeys. E.g. n=6, x=2 → 16.

items.q: The key-finding algorithm (start K = R, remove attributes while closure still = R) returns:
options: One candidate key (which one depends on removal order)
items.explain: It returns a single key; the result depends on the order attributes are removed. To get all candidate keys, use the essential-attributes method.

items.q: First Normal Form (1NF) requires that:
options: Every attribute holds only atomic (single) values — no composite/multivalued/nested
items.explain: 1NF disallows composite attributes, multivalued attributes, and nested relations — each cell must be a single atomic value.

items.q: Denormalization is:
options: Deliberately adding redundancy (storing a join) AFTER normalizing, to speed up reads
items.explain: Denormalization is an optimization applied after normalizing: accept some redundancy to avoid costly joins. Pros: faster reads; cons: costly updates, inconsistency risk, more storage.

items.q: A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and:
options: Every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the (whole) primary key
items.explain: 2NF = 1NF + no partial dependencies (every non-prime attribute depends on the whole key, not part of it).

items.q: R(P,Q,R,S,T), F = {PQ→R, S→T}, candidate key PQS. This relation is:
options: Not in 2NF — PQ→R and S→T are partial dependencies on the key PQS
items.explain: CK = PQS. PQ→R (R depends on part PQ) and S→T (T depends on part S) are partial dependencies of non-prime attributes → violates 2NF.

items.q: A relation in 2NF is in 3NF if:
options: No non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key
items.explain: 3NF = 2NF + no transitive dependency of a non-prime attribute on the key (no key → non-prime → non-prime chain).

items.q: The general definition of 3NF says whenever X → A holds, then:
options: X is a superkey AND A is prime
X is a superkey OR A is a prime attribute
items.explain: General 3NF: for every X→A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute. The 'A is prime' clause is what BCNF later removes.

items.q: The mnemonic 'the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key' refers to:
items.explain: 1NF = there is a key (atomic values); 2NF = depend on the WHOLE key (no partial dep); 3NF = depend on NOTHING BUT the key (no transitive dep).

items.q: In a 3NF check, a transitive chain prime → non-prime → prime is:
items.explain: 3NF's escape clause (b) allows X→A when A is prime. Only prime → non-prime → NON-prime (final attribute non-prime) violates 3NF.

items.q: A relation is in BCNF if whenever X → A holds:
items.explain: BCNF requires EVERY determinant to be a superkey — it drops 3NF's 'A is prime' allowance, making it strictly stronger.

items.q: A relation is in 3NF but NOT in BCNF exactly when there is an FD X → A with:
options: X a superkey and A prime
X NOT a superkey and A a prime attribute
items.explain: Such an FD satisfies 3NF (via 'A is prime') but violates BCNF (X is not a superkey). This is the only 3NF-not-BCNF situation.

items.q: TEACH(Student, Course, Instructor) with {Student,Course}→Instructor and Instructor→Course is in 3NF but not BCNF because:
options: Instructor→Course has a non-superkey determinant but Course is prime
items.explain: Instructor is not a superkey (violates BCNF), but Course is prime (so 3NF is satisfied). Classic 3NF-but-not-BCNF example.

items.q: Any relation with exactly two attributes is:
options: Always in BCNF regardless of its FDs
items.explain: With two attributes, any nontrivial FD's determinant must be a superkey, so a 2-attribute relation is always in BCNF (Elmasri 14.22, Silberschatz 7.36).

items.q: Between lossless join and dependency preservation, which MUST always be satisfied?
items.explain: Losslessness is non-negotiable — a lossy decomposition corrupts data. Dependency preservation is desirable but may be sacrificed (e.g. in BCNF).

items.q: The NJB test says a binary decomposition {R1,R2} of R is lossless iff:
items.explain: The shared attributes (R1∩R2) must functionally determine all of one of the pieces — i.e. be a key of at least one piece — for a lossless join.

items.q: Dependency preservation is guaranteed achievable up to which normal form?
items.explain: 3NF synthesis can preserve all dependencies AND be lossless. BCNF decomposition guarantees losslessness but may not preserve every FD.

items.q: Spurious tuples after joining a decomposition indicate:
options: A lossy join — the shared column wasn't a key of either piece
items.explain: Extra wrong rows mean the join didn't line up correctly — the common attribute didn't uniquely identify rows in either piece, so the decomposition is lossy.

items.q: A multivalued dependency X ↠ Y holds when:
options: For each X, the set of Y values is independent of the remaining attributes
Y is a subset of X
items.explain: An MVD models two independent multivalued facts: for a given X, Y values are independent of Z = R−(X∪Y), forcing every combination to appear.

items.q: A relation is in 4NF if, for every nontrivial MVD X ↠ Y:
items.explain: 4NF requires the determinant of every nontrivial MVD to be a superkey — analogous to BCNF but for multivalued dependencies.

items.q: An MVD is a special case of a join dependency with:
items.explain: A JD(R1,...,Rn) means R = R1 ⋈...⋈ Rn. An MVD X↠Y corresponds to decomposing into (X,Y) and (X,Z) — a JD with n=2.

items.q: Why is 5NF rarely used in practice?
options: Join dependencies are extremely hard to detect in real schemas
items.explain: JDs are nearly impossible to detect among hundreds of relations, so 5NF is mostly theoretical. Most commercial designs target 3NF/BCNF.

items.q: The correct order of the query-processing pipeline is:
options: Scan → parse → validate → build query tree → optimize → execute
items.explain: Scanner (tokens) → parser (syntax) → validation (names) → query tree → optimizer (plan) → code gen → runtime execution.

items.q: A semi-join (used to unnest EXISTS/IN) returns a left row:
options: For every match in the right table
As soon as it finds ONE match in the right table
items.explain: A semi-join returns a left row on the first match (no duplicates, no searching for all matches) — exactly EXISTS/IN semantics. NOT EXISTS maps to anti-join.

items.q: Which SELECT search method works only when the file is physically ordered on the key?
items.explain: Binary search needs an equality on a key the file is ordered by. Linear search always works; hash/primary index need those structures.

items.q: Which join algorithm sorts both inputs on the join attribute and merges them in a single pass?
items.explain: Sort-merge join sorts both relations on the join attribute then scans both once with two pointers — O(m+n) after the sort, avoiding nested loops.

items.q: The partition-hash join works by:
options: Hashing both tables into buckets (partition phase), then joining only matching buckets (probe phase)
items.explain: J4 partitions both relations with the same hash on the join attribute, then probes: only rows in the same bucket are compared, avoiding full-table comparison.

items.q: Why does `WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024` typically prevent index use?
options: Wrapping an indexed column in a function means the stored index values no longer match the comparison, forcing a full scan
items.explain: A function on an indexed column defeats the index (the index stores raw column values, not function outputs), so the engine must scan the whole table.

items.q: The MySQL EXPLAIN statement is used to:
options: Show how the engine plans to run a query (access order, index usage)
items.explain: EXPLAIN reveals the chosen execution plan — table access order, indexes used, estimated rows — so you can spot bottlenecks (e.g. full scans).

items.q: Adding a B-tree index on a filtered column typically changes a SELECT's cost from:
options: O(n) full scan to O(log n) index lookup
items.explain: Without an index the engine scans every row (O(n)); a B-tree index lets it jump to qualifying rows (O(log n)) — the biggest lever for SELECT performance on large tables.

items.q: Which is a recommended query-optimization technique?
options: Filter early with WHERE to limit rows before joins/aggregation
items.explain: Filtering early (and retrieving only needed columns, indexing join/filter columns, using LIMIT) reduces the rows every later step must process.
